sources.claim: A token can be a character, part of a word, a whole word or punctuation; ~4 characters; ~3/4 of a word; 100 tokens ≈ 75 words; reasoning models use internal reasoning tokens not shown as answer text
sources.note: OpenAI Help Center, 'Understanding and counting tokens'

sources.claim: Each text generation request is independent and stateless; multi-turn chat works by sending the previous messages back in with each request
GPT-3: 175 billion parameters, 96 layers, context window of 2048 tokens
sources.note: Brown et al. (2020), 'Language Models are Few-Shot Learners', abstract + Table 2.1 + §2.1

sources.claim: The Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, introduced in 2017
sources.note: Vaswani et al. (2017), 'Attention Is All You Need'

sources.claim: By default the API generates the entire output before sending it; streaming sends output as it is generated, over server-sent events
ChatGPT sometimes writes plausible-sounding but incorrect or nonsensical answers

lines.text: I don't understand | why nobody is talking about this.
When you press Enter on ChatGPT, | it has no idea | how its answer will end.
It writes one tiny piece at a time, | and it picks the next piece | only after the last one is out.
Here's everything that happens | after you press Enter.
First, your message gets *chopped*.
Not into words. | Into *tokens*. | Small chunks of text. | A token is about four characters, | or three quarters of a word.
But a model can't read letters. | So every token becomes a *number*.
Then each number becomes a long list of numbers, | a map of what it means.
Next, the part that surprises people. | It doesn't *remember* you.
Each request to the model starts from zero. | So your whole chat gets sent back in, | every single time.
And that has a limit. | GPT-3 could see two thousand and forty-eight tokens. | Past that, | it simply can't see.
Now the model reads it all. | Every token looks at every other token.
In, the cat sat because it was tired, | what does *it* point to? | The cat. | Attention figures that out.
This came from a twenty seventeen paper, | Attention Is All You Need. | It's the T in GPT. | *Transformer*.
And it doesn't do this once. | It stacks it.
GPT-3 had *ninety-six* layers, | and a hundred and seventy-five billion numbers | tuned during training.
Every layer sharpens the picture. | But after all that, | it still hasn't written a single word.
Quick thing. | This is exactly how I'm learning AI right now, on Teyro.
A few minutes a day, | and I use what I learn straight away. | Okay. | The first word.
At the very end, | the model gives every possible next token a *score*.
After, the sky is, | blue scores high. | Green scores low. | It picks one, | adds it to the text, | and runs the whole thing again.
Token. | Run. | Token. | Run. | Every piece is a full trip through the layers.
So why does it look like typing? | Because, sort of, it is.
Instead of waiting for the whole answer, | the app *streams* each piece to you | the moment it's made.
Here's the weird part. | There's no answer sitting in a database.
The model isn't looking anything up. | It's *predicting* what should come next.
That's why it can sound sure | and still be wrong. | OpenAI says so themselves.
To be fair, | newer models can think first, | in hidden tokens you never see. | But it's still tokens, | one at a time.
So. | Tokens. | Numbers. | Your whole chat, sent again. | Attention. | Layers. | One token at a time. | Streamed back.
I didn't get this from one video. | I learn all of it on Teyro.
There's an AI track. | Use AI tools, | build AI agents, | and create automations.
Lessons take a few minutes, | in four steps, | and you practise straight away, | with instant feedback.
My streak grows every day, | and a freeze covers a busy one. | Weekly leagues, | Bronze to Diamond. | Daily quests and chests.
Friends to race, | and a course community | that cheers your wins.
Now I don't just use AI. | I *build* with it.
It's not looking up an answer. | It's predicting the next *token*.
Want to understand AI like this? | Learn it on Teyro.
Search for it in your browser, | or go straight to Teyro dot app.
